title: Changing Roles and Identities in a Teacher-Driven Professional Development Community
extended_summary:
This paper examines how a teacher-driven professional development community, Streamline to Mastery, changed teachers’ participation, leadership, and identities over time. The central question is whether a professional learning environment built around teacher agency, shared inquiry, and skeptical discourse can foster a community of practice in which teachers move from peripheral participation to more central, expert-like roles.

The program was not a generative AI intervention; rather, it was a long-term professional development model for secondary physics and physical science teachers. Teachers were responsible for setting their own goals, planning classroom action research, sharing lessons, designing workshops, and preparing conference presentations. The research team observed the program through videos of meetings, email threads, and interviews/focus groups, and coded these data to track agenda setting, email initiation, and instances of challenge/disagreement in discussion.

The sample included four teachers from two urban high schools in high-needs districts in the United States. Teachers met with researchers every other week in 2.5- to 3-hour evening sessions in teachers’ classrooms. The study found that teachers increasingly initiated emails, set meeting agendas, and challenged one another’s ideas, indicating a shift from researcher-led professional development to a more egalitarian community of expert learners.

The authors conclude that professional development may be more effective when it creates conditions for teacher agency and community formation rather than simply delivering outside expertise. They argue that teacher knowledge and resources already reside within teachers’ everyday practice, and that vulnerability, skepticism, and shared inquiry can support both individual and collective growth.
